# Turnaround-or-Exit Assessment: Industrial Services Unit

*This assessment is respectfully offered for the board's deliberation. It builds on the genuine savings delivered by the two prior restructurings — the persistence of losses despite that good work tells us the diagnosis was incomplete, not that the effort was misplaced. One question guides everything below: **for whom are these assets worth the most, and what would have to be true for that to be us?***

---

## Executive Summary

**Provisional diagnosis (to be evidenced, not assumed):** A mixed condition — structural erosion in parts of the portfolio (sub-scale service density, declining end-markets) compounded by execution wounds that are ours to heal (pricing discipline, legacy underpriced contracts, an allocation-distorted P&L, and a talent drain that is itself a verdict on the unit's prospects). The prior restructurings treated a revenue-and-mix disease with cost medicine; the losses continued because the cause was never only cost.

**Proposed definition of success** (the board's test, operationalized): by month 12, the unit demonstrates **run-rate EBITDA breakeven** (final quarter annualized), **book-to-bill ≥ 1.0 in the retained perimeter for two consecutive quarters**, achieved **within a pre-agreed funding envelope**, with a credible year-two path toward group hurdle returns. Baselines are set in the first 30 days; all gate thresholds below are expressed against them.

**Recommendation:** Run a **dual track from day one** — a gated turnaround on a *narrowed perimeter*, with exit preparation proceeding quietly in parallel under a separate, firewalled team. Within a one-year clock, sequential logic ("fix first, sell later") guarantees a weak negotiating position in month 11. Gate thresholds are agreed in writing **now**, so that month 12 is a decision rather than a debate.

**The fork:** If the 60-day diagnostic finds no structurally viable core, we would respectfully propose not spending the year on a third restructuring. Spend it maximizing exit value and protecting the people and customer relationships the group will carry forward.

---

## 1. Diagnosis: Structural or Execution?

### 1.1 What the Known Facts Already Suggest

| Signal | What It Suggests | What Would Confirm or Refute |
|---|---|---|
| Three years of losses despite two *successful* cost programs | The disease is revenue, mix, and footprint — not cost. Cuts may also have removed revenue-generating capacity, deepening the decline | Restated standalone P&L; revenue-per-head before/after each restructuring; analysis of which roles were cut |
| Shrinking order book | Demand erosion, lost competitiveness, or (benignly) deliberate walk-away from bad work | Book-to-bill by segment for 8 quarters; win/loss review of last 50 bids; end-market growth data |
| Best managers transferring out | An internal verdict on the unit's prospects; execution capability hollowing at the moment it is most needed | Exit/transfer interviews; regretted-loss inventory; where they went and why |
| Customers shared with profitable divisions | Entanglement cuts both ways: hidden subsidy *or* hidden value; exit could damage group accounts | Overlap mapping; arm's-length transfer-pricing review; joint account interviews |
| Reported losses may be allocation-distorted | Standalone economics may be better — or worse — than reported | P&L restated net of corporate allocations at arm's-length rates |

### 1.2 Structural vs. Execution: The Classification Test

Each loss driver identified by the diagnostic is classified before any plan is built:

| Loss Driver (hypotheses) | Structural If… | Execution If… | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dispersed, low-density territories | No path to profitable route density at attainable share | Density achievable by pruning footprint | Jobs-per-technician-day by territory vs. breakeven threshold |
| Legacy underpriced maintenance contracts | — | Repriceable or exitable at renewal | Contract-level margin review, top 20 contracts |
| Corporate allocation burden | — | A reporting artifact, not an economic one | Restated standalone P&L |
| Declining end-market segments | Market shrinking faster than share can be gained | — | Independent market data |
| Weak pricing discipline | — | Fixable via floor pricing and bid governance | Bid-level margin analysis |
| Talent drain | — | Fixable, but time-critical | Retention plan effectiveness (Section 4.1) |

**Rule:** a segment or service line is *structural-exit* if no path to acceptable margin exists at attainable density and share; *execution-fix* if margin is achievable through pricing, mix, and utilization within 12 months. Only execution-fix economics belong in the turnaround perimeter.
